## CHAPTER VIII

DIPLOMACY (1861)

Hardly a week passed when the newspapers announced that President Lincoln had selected Charles Francis Adams as his Minister to England. Once more, silently, Henry put Blackstone back on its shelf. Time had passed! The law, altogether, as path of education, vanished in April, 1861, leaving a million young men planted in the mud of a lawless world, to begin a new life without education at all. Mr. Adams intimated that he thought himself entitled to the services of one of his sons, and indicated Henry as the only one who could be spared. Henry packed his trunk again without a word.

Ridiculous as he knew himself about to be in his new rôle, he was less ridiculous than his betters. He knew his father's appointment was the result of Governor Seward's personal friendship; he did not then know that Senator Sumner had opposed it. That Mr. Adams was unfit might well be, since it was hard to find a fit appointment in the list of possible candidates, except Mr. Sumner himself; and the weakest of all Mr. Adams's proofs of fitness was his consent to quit a safe seat in Congress for an exceedingly unsafe seat in London. In the family history, its members had taken many a dangerous risk, but never before had they taken one so desperate.

The President and Secretary of State knew least of all. The Secretary of Legation was a Chicago newspaper editor who had not a thought of staying in the post; the Assistant Secretary was inherited from Buchanan's time, a hard worker, but socially useless. Mr. Adams made no effort to find efficient help.

On April 13 the storm burst and rolled several hundred thousand young men like Henry Adams into the surf of a wild ocean, to be beaten about for four years by the waves of war. He had time to watch the regiments form ranks before Boston State House and march southward, and to go down the harbor to see his brother Charles quartered in Fort Independence before being thrown into the furnace of the Army of the Potomac. Few things were for the moment so trivial in importance as the solitary private secretary crawling down to the wretched old Cunard steamer Niagara at East Boston to start again for Liverpool. This time the pitcher of education had gone to the fountain once too often; it was fairly broken; and the young man had got to meet a hostile world without defence—or arms.

Minister Adams sailed for England, May 1, 1861, with much the same outfit as Admiral Dupont would have enjoyed if the Government had sent him to attack Port Royal with one cabin-boy in a rowboat. The cabin-boy was the most fortunate person in the party, having for master only his father, who never fretted, never dictated, never disciplined, and whose idea of American diplomacy was that of the eighteenth century. Minister Adams remembered how his grandfather had sailed from Mount Wollaston in midwinter, 1778, on the little frigate Boston, taking his eleven-year-old son John Quincy with him, for secretary, on a diplomacy of adventure that had hardly a parallel for success. He remembered how John Quincy, in 1809, had sailed for Russia, with himself, a baby of two years old, to cope with Napoleon and the Czar Alexander single-handed. He thought it natural that the Government should send him out as an adventurer also, with a twenty-three-year-old son, and he did not even notice that he left not a friend behind him. For the first time America was posing as the champion of legitimacy and order; but the only rag of legitimacy in the mission was the private secretary, whose stature was not sufficient to impose awe on the Court and Parliament of Great Britain.

The private secretary could not grumble to his chief. He never labored so hard to learn a language as he did to hold his tongue, and it affected him for life. He was already an adept when the party landed at Liverpool, May 13, 1861, and went instantly up to London: a family of early Christian martyrs about to be flung into an arena of lions, under the glad eyes of Tiberius Palmerston.

Then came the Trent Affair: the seizure of Mason and Slidell brought the Legation to the brink of war, and the Minister, summoned from Yorkshire, met the crisis without losing his nerve. The shock passed; the secretaries learned that patience, silence, and the closing of newspaper indiscretions were the only diplomacy left to them.
